title: Counting Important Terms · Level 3
slo: Explain how frequency analysis and TF-IDF identify document topics.

exercises.question_text: Which frequent terms could suggest a passage is about AI business benefits? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: This is one of the frequent normalized terms in the passage. It helps signal the subject.
This frequent term helps identify the business focus. Counts of such terms can indicate themes.
This term appears frequently after preparation. It supports the theme of benefits.

options.error_type: Confuses a scoring method with a frequent document term
options.rationale: IDF is a measure, not one of the frequent passage terms. It measures rarity across a collection.
options.better_fit: Choose this when naming the collection-wide rarity measure.

feedback.intrinsic: You would label the method instead of identifying a topic clue.
feedback.instructional: Look for the frequently occurring content terms, not the name of a scoring measure.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Frequent content terms can point to a passage’s topic.

exercises.question_text: Why can raw frequency be weak for distinguishing documents in a large corpus?

options.text: Many terms appear in many documents
options.rationale: Widely shared terms describe a general theme. They do not identify a specific item’s topic.
Terms can be counted as tokens. The limitation is that shared counts may not distinguish items.
options.better_fit: This would fit a situation where no tokenization data was available, which is not the issue here.

feedback.intrinsic: You would miss useful counts that still reveal shared themes.
feedback.instructional: Raw frequency can count terms; its weakness is that many terms may be common across the collection.

options.rationale: Tokens can be assigned discrete numeric identifiers. Their occurrences can then be counted.
options.better_fit: This does not fit the described token-counting process.

feedback.intrinsic: You would reject information that can be counted.
feedback.instructional: Assigned token values make counting occurrences straightforward; shared terms are the real limitation.

options.rationale: Frequent terms can suggest themes. The issue is distinguishing one specific topic from another.
options.better_fit: This does not fit frequency analysis, which can reveal general themes.

feedback.intrinsic: You would lose the useful shared-theme insight from the collection.
feedback.instructional: Common terms can still show a broad theme, even when they cannot distinguish individual items.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Shared terms describe a broad theme but not each specific topic.

exercises.question_text: Put the pieces in the correct order.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The idea would be harder to follow in a workplace discussion.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with the frequent terms, state where they appear, then state what they reveal.

exercises.correct_answer: Frequent normalized terms in one document can suggest a document's topic
exercises.explanation: The frequent normalized terms are the evidence, and their location in one item makes them useful as a topic clue.

exercises.question_text: Across many documents, raw word frequency is less useful because shared terms do not ___ one document from another.

feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The issue with shared terms is that they do not distinguish or differentiate individual items.

exercises.explanation: A widely shared term can show a broad theme, but it cannot separate individual topics. Summarizing, classifying, and tokenizing are different tasks.

exercises.question_text: A product writer must label two articles: one about declarative AI-agent creation in Copilot Studio and one about code-based development in Microsoft Foundry. Which terms are strong TF-IDF candidates for identifying the specific topics? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Copilot is specific to the Copilot Studio topic. It has strong distinguishing value.
Declarative identifies the configured-not-programmed approach. It distinguishes that topic from code-based development.
Foundry identifies the code-based development topic. It is specific to that sample.

options.error_type: Chooses a shared term with zero IDF
options.rationale: Microsoft appears in both samples. In the two-item collection, its IDF is zero.
options.better_fit: Choose this when naming the shared broad theme.

feedback.intrinsic: The labels would remain too similar to identify the separate focuses.
feedback.instructional: Strong TF-IDF candidates are frequent in one item but relatively rare in the others.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These terms help identify the specific topics because they are not shared by both articles.

options.rationale: TF is the number of times a term appears in one item. Six appearances give a TF of 6.
Collection-wide rarity is IDF. TF is only the within-item count.

feedback.intrinsic: You would confuse a local count with collection-wide rarity.
feedback.instructional: TF counts appearances in one item; IDF checks how widely the term appears.

options.rationale: TF-IDF is the combined score. TF is one input to that calculation.
options.better_fit: Choose this when TF is multiplied by IDF.

feedback.intrinsic: You would skip the distinction between a count and a combined score.
feedback.instructional: TF is the count; TF-IDF combines that count with IDF.

options.rationale: Sentence connection scores belong to TextRank. TF counts term appearances.
options.better_fit: Choose this when ranking connected sentences for a summary.

feedback.intrinsic: You would analyze sentence links instead of term occurrences.
feedback.instructional: TF is a simple term count in one item.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TF is simply the number of appearances in one item.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the following steps to calculate IDF.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The calculation would no longer follow the IDF formula.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Find N and df(t) first, divide N by df(t), then take the logarithm.

exercises.correct_answer: Count all documents Find documents containing t Divide N by df(t) Take the logarithm
exercises.explanation: IDF needs both collection counts before forming N/df(t). The logarithm is applied after the ratio is calculated.

exercises.question_text: A documentation analyst reviews many Microsoft AI-agent articles. The articles share words such as “AI,” “Microsoft,” and “agent,” but the analyst must identify each article's specific topic. Which approach fits best?

options.rationale: TF-IDF discounts widely shared terms through IDF. It highlights terms frequent in one item but relatively rare in others.

options.error_type: Confuses shared frequency with document-specific relevance
options.rationale: Raw frequency can show broad themes but shared words do not separate individual topics. It lacks the rarity component.
options.better_fit: Choose this for a quick clue from one item.

feedback.intrinsic: The review would keep surfacing the same shared words.
feedback.instructional: When many items share terms, use TF-IDF to give more weight to distinctive terms.

options.rationale: TF counts occurrences in one item only. It cannot reduce the weight of terms shared across the collection.
options.better_fit: Choose this when only within-item appearances matter.

feedback.intrinsic: A heavily repeated shared word could look more distinctive than it is.
feedback.instructional: TF-IDF adds IDF so common collection-wide terms receive less weight.

options.rationale: IDF measures rarity across the collection. It does not show how often a rare term appears in the individual item.
options.better_fit: Choose this when measuring rarity alone.

feedback.intrinsic: A rare term could be emphasized even if it barely appears in the item.
feedback.instructional: TF-IDF combines IDF with TF, so it reflects both rarity and local frequency.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TF-IDF combines local frequency with collection-wide rarity to identify specific topics.

exercises.question_text: If a term appears six times in a document, its IDF is 6.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A within-item count would be assigned to the wrong measure.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: TF counts appearances in one item. IDF measures rarity across the collection.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Six appearances give TF of 6, not IDF.

exercises.question_text: Which facts describe Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: IDF checks whether a term is common or rare across a collection. Rarer terms have more distinguishing value.

options.text: It uses total document count N
options.rationale: N is the total number of items in the IDF formula. It is divided by df(t).

options.text: A term in every document has IDF zero
options.rationale: When df(t) equals N, the ratio is 1. The logarithm of 1 is zero.

options.text: It counts uses in one document
options.rationale: Counting uses in one item is TF. IDF depends on how many items contain the term.

feedback.intrinsic: You would mistake a collection measure for a local count.
feedback.instructional: IDF uses N and df(t); TF counts appearances in one item.

exercises.explanation: Correct. IDF reflects how widely a term occurs across a collection.
